title: First Passage and First Return Times
breadcrumb: Stochastic processes → Markov chains → First Passage and First Return Times
engineName: Use state diagrams, first-step equations and exact checks to solve Markov-chain problems.
objectives: Define the relevant Markov-chain quantity and interpret it correctly.
Set up equations using the transition matrix and the correct boundary conditions.
Solve finite-state examples exactly and verify the result.
Recognise assumptions, limiting cases and common UGC NET examination traps.

prereq.name: Markov property
prereq.why: The conditional future depends on the present state.

prereq.name: Linear equations and gcd
prereq.why: First-step equations and period calculations use these tools.

traps: Do not confuse first passage with occupancy at a fixed time.
Do not forget that the target has zero remaining hitting time.
A hitting probability must lie in [0,1]; a mean time need not be an integer.
Communication is mutual reachability; a one-way path is insufficient.
A closed class has no outgoing transition.
Period is a gcd, not the smallest return time.
howto: Draw the transition graph first. Mark the target or communicating class, write the relevant definition, and then calculate. Try each scene's question before opening its explanation. Finish by checking the result against the original transition structure.

sheet: First passage is the first arrival at a target state.
First return starts in the target and requires n≥1.
Expected hitting time has boundary hⱼ=0.
The first-step equation counts the transition taken now.
An expected time can be non-integer or infinite.
cards: Specify the target state and stopping rule.
Condition on the state after one transition.
Remaining hitting time at the target is zero.
Each state must be reachable from the other.
GCD of possible positive return times.
tricks: For a hitting-time equation, count the first step explicitly.
Use gcd for periodicity; do not use the minimum return time.
shortcuts: A self-loop makes the period one.
An absorbing state is a closed singleton class.
In a finite chain, closed communicating classes are recurrent.
remember: First-passage probability and expected first-passage time are different quantities.
Recurrence and aperiodicity are separate properties.

scenes.title: Tools and notation
scenes.objective: Refresh the probability and algebra needed for first-step analysis.
body: A Markov chain moves between states according to its transition matrix. A hitting-time question asks when a specified target is reached, not merely where the chain is at a selected time.
For expected hitting time hᵢ, count the transition taken now, then add the expected remaining time from the next state.

items.recall: The probability that the next state is j given that the current state is i.
refresh: The first index is the current state.
The second index is the destination.

items.ask: Why condition on the first transition?
items.recall: It separates mutually exclusive next-state possibilities.
refresh: Multiply its probability by the continuation quantity.

items.ask: What is the remaining hitting time when the target is already reached?

ask.q: What must be identified before writing a hitting-time equation?
ask.nudge: Name the target and define exactly when the experiment stops.

scenes.title: First arrival is not ordinary occupancy
scenes.objective: Distinguish first passage from being in a state at a fixed time.
body: A system may enter a target state, leave it, and later return. The first-passage time records the first arrival only.
A return time starts in the state of interest and asks for the first positive time at which the chain returns.

scenario.teaser: A machine reaches a repair-complete state
scenario.title: When does the machine first become ready?
body: A machine moves through operating states before reaching the repair-complete state. The manager asks for the number of transitions until the first arrival at repair-complete. If the chain later leaves that state, the first-passage time does not change.
scenario.q: Does a later departure change the first-passage time?
scenario.answer: No. The first-passage time is fixed at the first arrival.

ask.q: How does a first-return time differ from first passage from outside the target?
ask.nudge: A return starts in the target and uses a positive time index.

scenes.title: Definitions and first-step equations
scenes.objective: Write the first-passage probability and expected-time equations.

blocks.body: Tⱼ=inf{n≥0:Xₙ=j} when the chain starts outside the target.
hⱼ=0; for i≠j, hᵢ=1+Σₖpᵢₖhₖ, when the expectation is finite.
For gᵢ=Pᵢ(Tⱼ<∞), set gⱼ=1 and gᵢ=Σₖpᵢₖgₖ for i≠j.

flow.title: First-step workflow
flow.alt: Define target, condition on next state, solve and check.

ask.q: What is the boundary value for expected remaining time at the target?
ask.nudge: The target has already been reached.

scenes.title: Worked example: a symmetric two-state route
scenes.objective: Solve expected time to an absorbing target.
scenes.problem: From state 1 the chain moves to state 2 with probability 1/2 and to absorbing target 3 with probability 1/2. From state 2 it moves to state 1 with probability 1/2 and to state 3 with probability 1/2. Find the mean time to hit 3.

steps.why: No remaining transitions are needed at the target.

steps.say: Condition on the first step from state 1.
steps.why: The first transition is counted even when the target is reached immediately.

ask.q: What is the expected hitting time from state 1?

scenes.title: Guided example: a self-loop
scenes.objective: Account for time spent in a non-target state.
scenes.problem: From state 1, move to target 3 with probability 1/4 and to state 2 with probability 3/4. From state 2, move to target 3 with probability 1/2 and remain at 2 with probability 1/2. Find h₁ and h₂.

steps.why: A self-loop still consumes one step.

ask.q: Why does the self-loop increase the expected time?

scenes.title: Probability of hitting versus expected time
scenes.objective: Distinguish a hitting probability from a mean hitting time.
body: A hitting probability is between zero and one. An expected hitting time is measured in transitions and may be non-integer or infinite.
For a hitting probability gᵢ, the target boundary is gⱼ=1. For expected remaining time hᵢ, the target boundary is hⱼ=0.

scenario.teaser: A short route to a target
scenario.title: Guaranteed arrival within two steps
body: From state 1 the chain moves to state 2 with probability 1/3 and to target 3 with probability 2/3. State 2 moves to state 3 with probability one. Every possible path reaches the target within two transitions.
scenario.q: What is the probability of hitting 3 within two steps?
scenario.answer: One, because both possible first-step branches reach 3 by the second transition.

ask.q: Which boundary value belongs to a hitting probability at the target?
ask.nudge: The event of having hit the target is certain there.

scenes.title: Common first-passage traps
scenes.objective: Avoid boundary, indexing and interpretation errors.

items.q: What is the boundary condition for expected hitting time?
What is the boundary condition for hitting probability?
Does a self-loop consume a transition?
items.a: Yes. It contributes one step in an expected hitting-time equation.

ask.q: What range check applies to a hitting probability?
ask.nudge: It is a probability, so it cannot exceed one or be negative.

scenes.title: Recall the method
scenes.objective: Recall definitions and equations without looking back.

items.q: State the expected hitting-time first-step equation.
items.a: hᵢ=1+Σₖpᵢₖhₖ for non-target i, with hⱼ=0.
gᵢ=Σₖpᵢₖgₖ for non-target i, with gⱼ=1.
The first positive time n≥1 at which the chain returns to its starting state.

ask.q: Which equation would you use if the question asks for a mean number of steps?
ask.nudge: Use h, include the first step, and set the target value to zero.

scenes.title: Worked example: guaranteed arrival
scenes.objective: Verify a simple exact hitting-time result.
scenes.problem: From state 1, move to state 2 with probability 1/3 and to target 3 with probability 2/3. State 2 moves to 3 with probability one. Find the mean hitting time from state 1.

steps.say: Write the target and intermediate equations.
Condition on the first step from state 1.
steps.why: The two branches have probabilities 1/3 and 2/3.
The direct-hit branch has zero remaining time.

ask.q: Why is the answer not an integer?
ask.nudge: It is an expectation over paths of different lengths.

scenes.title: Exam summary
scenes.objective: Consolidate the equations and boundary values.
body: First-passage time is the first arrival at a target; first-return time starts in the target and requires n≥1.
For expected hitting time: hⱼ=0 and hᵢ=1+Σₖpᵢₖhₖ. For hitting probability: gⱼ=1 and gᵢ=Σₖpᵢₖgₖ.
Check that probabilities lie in [0,1], expected times are nonnegative, and every equation matches the transition graph.

ask.q: What is the key difference between the two boundary values?
ask.nudge: Expected remaining time is zero; probability of having hit is one.
